title: There or not there? A multidisciplinary review and research agenda on the impact of transparent barriers on human perception, action, and social behavior
review_question: To explore the extent to which transparent barriers, simultaneously 'there and not there' architecturally, are actually 'there and/or not there' from perceptual, behavioral, and social points of view, and their impact on human cognition and action.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Studies were identified by searching Google Scholar and Scopus for terms related to 'glass architecture,' 'transparency perception/detection,' 'transparent barrier AND distance/privacy/space.' Included material referred to human cognition/behavior, elucidated architectural, perceptual, navigational, or social aspects of transparent barrier use, and was representative of major research lines.

findings.antecedent: Transparent barriers (visual cues: glossiness, highlights, diffusion, refraction, coloring, luminance differences, contour junctions)
findings.quote: the visual perception of transparent barriers seems largely guided by perceivers' experience-based expectations of where to find them... and the detection of visual cues that signal the presence of an invisible structure are of essential importance.

findings.antecedent: Specific luminance differences between neighboring parts of a surface (photometric cues)
findings.quote: Metelli demonstrated that specific luminance differences between neighboring parts of a surface would induce the impression that some parts were seen directly, whereas others were seen through a transparent layer.
contours aligned in the way of an X-junction... indicate transparency... Whereas T-junctions typically imply occlusion.

findings.antecedent: Undetected transparent barriers (clear, smooth, faultless, frameless glass)
findings.quote: Unsurprisingly, undetected transparent barriers can pose a serious health and safety risk. Accidents due to collisions with glass doors or walls have been reported.
the ability to perceive transparency seems to be actively acquired during the first months of one's life.
transparent barrier can confine an individual to a limited physical space... while simultaneously providing visual access to a larger space.

findings.antecedent: Conflicting tactile and visual information (transparent barrier), especially within peripersonal space
findings.quote: when faced with conflicting information coming from tactile and visual sensors, humans rely more strongly on the latter, especially when the sensory contradictions arise within a person's peripersonal space.

findings.consequent: Basic reflexes (startle, withdrawal, tactile extinction) toward approaching objects/people
findings.quote: the patients' automatic representation of their peripersonal space is unaffected by the presence of the barrier. Thus, the mere knowledge that actual touch is impossible does not modulate the observed extinction effect.
children younger than 10 months of age tried to directly reach for toys 'through' transparent surfaces, even though they readily reached around opaque barriers.

findings.antecedent: Transparent barriers (for infants up to 10 months)
findings.quote: up to 10-months of age, infants displayed significant difficulty in detour ability when obstructed by a transparent barrier.
This response pattern does not seem to result from an inability to see the barrier, but rather from a flawed assumption that transparent barriers can be physically penetrated.

findings.antecedent: Transparent barriers vs. opaque barriers (for toddlers)
findings.quote: Both 12- and 18-month-olds were found to successfully cross opaque barriers at larger thresholds than transparent barriers, suggesting that a child's ability to perform an adequate motor response suffers when faced with transparency.

findings.antecedent: Transparent barrier over visual cliff (for infants)
findings.quote: infants capable of crawling typically hesitated to cross the surface, despite encouragement from a parent on the other side of the cliff.
When entering such walkways, many visitors hesitate to step forward, despite witnessing other people standing or moving around on the same structure.

findings.consequent: Overcoming visual illusion of penetrability (transparent barriers)
findings.quote: overcoming this overreliance on visual information in the presence of transparent barriers does not only seem to require extensive practice, but also consistent awareness of the problem at hand.

findings.antecedent: Transparent environments (for individuals with cognitive decline, e.g., Alzheimer patients)
findings.quote: People suffering from cognitive decline, such as Alzheimer patients, have been found to cope poorly with transparent environments.

findings.source: The Impact of Transparent Barriers on Social Behavior
findings.quote: Transparent barriers form unique kinds of barriers, given that they separate space physically, but not visually.

findings.consequent: Assumption of unimpaired visual information transmission
findings.source: The Impact of Transparent Barriers on Social Behavior
findings.quote: Thus, both children and adults assume that a physical separation through a transparent barrier does not interfere with the transmission of visual information.

findings.source: The Impact of Transparent Barriers on Social Behavior
findings.quote: confined spaces defined by non-transparent barriers seem to encourage aggression, rather than withdrawal, during stressful social encounters.

findings.antecedent: Brighter rooms (lighting conditions around transparent barriers)
findings.consequent: Social inhibition (reduced anti-social behavior, increased prosocial behavior)
findings.source: The Impact of Transparent Barriers on Social Behavior
findings.quote: Brighter rooms, for instance, seem to facilitate social inhibition... an effect that can reduce anti-social behavior... but also prosocial behavior.

findings.consequent: Novelty, requirement for active cognitive construction of presence
findings.quote: Not only are such barriers unique in their dual nature... but they also form a novel type of environmental structure from an evolutionary point of view.
initial observations suggest that openness and transparency in workplace settings can facilitate productivity and innovation by enhancing the exchange of knowledge and skills between individuals.

findings.consequent: User-driven modifications (covering glass) due to privacy/territoriality needs
findings.quote: employees' preferences and demands for privacy and defensible territories may interfere with architectural ideals of transparency... Anecdotal evidence reveals that... non-transparent items are often strategically placed to cover facades and interior walls made of glass.

findings.antecedent: Differential preferences for transparency (architects vs. users)
findings.consequent: Lethargy and concentration difficulties (sick building syndrome)
findings.quote: Differential preferences for transparency between architects and users may contribute to lethargy and difficulties concentrating as discussed in the context of the so-called sick building syndrome.

findings.antecedent: Architectural design features (e.g., windowed view to natural setting)
findings.quote: The results showed faster, less painful recovery for surgical patients with a windowed view to a natural setting than for those with a view of a brick wall.

synthesis_conclusions: Transparent barriers pose a unique challenge to the human visual system, requiring active detection and integration of multiple visual features, and their non-detection is common, leading to unintentional collisions.

Very young children and individuals with cognitive decline struggle with navigating transparent structures, indicating that the human mind must actively construe the presence of such entities through experience and retrieval.

Despite a cognitive understanding of transparent barriers as solid separators of space, healthy adults occasionally treat them as if they are not there, with reflexive responses and high-stake transactions revealing a tendency to prioritize visual information over tactile experience or explicit knowledge.

This overreliance on visual penetrability can override tactile experience and explicit knowledge, impacting distance estimation and potentially social behavior (e.g., privacy, crowding, territoriality, and interpersonal involvement).

Systematic, cross-disciplinary research combining the expertise of architects, designers, and behavioral scientists is essential to develop detailed recommendations and guidelines for the architectural use of transparent barriers.
evidence_gaps: How and when the visual system establishes expertise with transparent structures or certain informative cues signaling their presence.
Whether frequent exposure to transparent barriers may facilitate a perceiver's ability to spontaneously detect relevant visual cues.
Whether and to which extent distraction interferes with a person's capacity to perceive transparent materials.
Whether frequent exposure to and experience with transparent barriers may alter mechanisms of multisensory integration and/or people's spontaneous responses (habituation).
How much exposure to transparent barriers does it generally take until habituation is noticeable.
Do some people habituate more or less quickly when shielded by a transparent barrier than others and if so, why.
Can habituation effects be transferred across different settings.
Would the habituation of reflexes behind a transparent barrier ultimately compromise a person's rapid responses in settings that lack such barriers.
How and to what extent the improvement in understanding transparent barriers as impenetrable entities takes place as humans grow older.
To what extent a separation of strangers by a transparent barrier impacts social behavior.
Whether people's need for controlling their involvement with others depends on the presence or absence of transparent barriers.
How transparent barriers affect tacit norms of looking behavior (e.g., staring longer).
Whether targets of prolonged looks may be more comfortable with attracting someone's gaze through a transparent barrier than when no barrier is present.
Whether people consider spaces largely defined by transparent barriers as confined or open.
Whether transparent barriers reduce feelings of crowding in spaces by increasing perceived spaciousness.
Whether transparent barriers influence readiness to aggress or withdraw during perceived social threat, depending on stress-reducing or stress-inducing views.
Can beneficial consequences of social proximity (e.g., inhibition of stress hormones) occur across transparent barriers.
Are spaces bounded by transparent barriers sufficient to fulfill privacy needs.
To what degree can transparent barriers define a territory that is recognized by others.
Can spaces defined by transparent barriers influence social interactions via changes in environmental features, such as lighting conditions and the level of visual stimulation.
In which kinds of environments transparent barriers are likely to act as stressors or healers.
The versatile cognitive and behavioral responses that humans adopt upon encountering and inhabiting transparent environments.
How transparent barriers impact human functioning across different behavior settings.
The extent to which synomorphic mechanisms arise from environments with transparent barriers.

Whether people with chronically low privacy needs, reduced impression management concerns, low territoriality claims, and/or claustrophobic tendencies experience greater satisfaction in surroundings with transparent barriers.
Whether the use of glass features in architecture might be most welcome by occupants from cultures that are willing to publicize their everyday lives.
limitations: The current knowledge base suffers from a lack of systematic empirical investigations into the human response to transparent barriers, undermining the ability to predict how people orient themselves in glass environments and optimize their architectural use.

paper_metadata.title: How universal is preference for visual curvature? A systematic review and meta‐analysis
paper_metadata.journal: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
paper_metadata.crossref_title: How universal is preference for visual curvature? A systematic review and meta‐analysis
paper_metadata.crossref_journal: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Evidence dating back a century shows that humans are sensitive to and exhibit a preference for visual curvature. This effect has been observed in different age groups, human cultures, and primate species, suggesting that a preference for curvature could be universal. At the same time, several studies have found that preference for curvature is modulated by contextual and individual factors, casting doubt on this hypothesis. To resolve these conflicting findings, we conducted a systematic meta‐analysis of studies that have investigated the preference for visual curvature. Our meta‐analysis included 61 studies which provided 106 independent samples and 309 effect sizes. The results of a three‐level random effects model revealed a Hedges’
                    g
                    of 0.39—consistent with a medium effect size. Further analyses revealed that preference for curvature is moderated by four factors: presentation time, stimulus type, expertise, and task. Together, our results suggest that preference for visual curvature is a reliable but not universal phenomenon and is influenced by factors other than perceptual information.
